name: Crystal healing

card.summary: A New Age practice of placing or wearing stones such as rose quartz or amethyst, which practitioners use as part of beauty and wellness routines aimed at a calmer, brighter, more rested look.
card.note: Some stones (e.g. shungite) contain heavy metals; crystals are not a substitute for medical care.

quick.overview:
Crystal healing is the practice of holding, wearing or placing stones on the body, chosen by colour or perceived properties, to balance what practitioners call energy. In appearance circles it shows up as rose quartz and jade facial rollers, crystal-infused skincare, gemstone jewellery and meditation routines meant to reduce stress, which practitioners link to a fresher complexion and better sleep.

Practitioners describe effects such as lifted mood and reduced tension. A controlled experiment reported by Wikipedia (French and colleagues) gave volunteers real or look-alike quartz to meditate with and found similar reported effects in both groups; researchers conclude outcomes track expectation rather than the mineral.
quick.how: People keep stones on a desk or bedside, wear them as jewellery, place them on the body during relaxation or meditation, or use stone-shaped facial tools in a skincare routine, often alongside practices such as reiki or aromatherapy. Practitioners typically describe using them as an ongoing habit.
quick.risks: Handling smooth stones is generally low-risk. Some minerals, such as shungite, can contain heavy metals, and Wikipedia notes toxicity concerns with prolonged handling or ingestion. Crystal mining in places like Madagascar has been reported to involve unsafe informal work. Clinicians advise that crystal use not replace medical treatment.

lead: Crystal healing is a New Age practice in which stones and minerals are held, worn or placed on the body in the belief that they balance or direct subtle energy.[1][2] Practitioners pick stones by colour, shape or traditional associations, and the practice is often combined with reiki, flower essences or homeopathy.[2]

In looksmaxxing and beauty settings, crystal use mostly serves as a wellness and relaxation layer: stones such as rose quartz or amethyst are kept nearby, worn, or built into facial tools and skincare rituals. The appearance chain proponents describe runs from calmer mood and better rest to a fresher, less tense look.

Researchers have tested the practice in placebo-controlled settings. A 1999 study by French and Williams reported that volunteers given real quartz or an indistinguishable placebo stone reported similar crystal effects, and a 2001 review concluded no evidence of effect beyond placebo.[2] Retail sales were estimated above US$1 billion per year in 2019.[2]

chain: Stones worn, held or used as facial tools
Relaxation ritual and perceived stress relief
angle.text: People incorporate crystals into skincare and wind-down routines, using stone rollers or keeping stones nearby. Proponents say the resulting relaxation shows in a fresher face; any visible effect is attributed by researchers to relaxation and expectation.

infobox: Over US$1 billion per year retail (2019 estimate)[2]

paras: Practitioners say crystals can raise low energy, release blocked energy or protect against negative energy.[2] Stones are placed on or near the body, worn, or used in meditation. The word "crystal" comes from the Greek for ice; ancient Greeks believed clear quartz was permanently frozen water, and ancient Egyptians wore stone amulets for protection.[2]

Beauty applications include rose quartz and jade facial rollers, gemstone-infused products, crystal-set jewellery, and sleep-environment items such as crystal plates built into heated beds (a Korean patent describes such a bed combining thermotherapy with crystal plates).[3] Users describe these as part of self-care routines intended to relax the face and reduce visible tiredness.

No clinical trials have shown crystal healing to produce physiological or cosmetic effects. In the 1999 experiment cited by Wikipedia, 80 volunteers meditated with real or placebo quartz and reported typical crystal effects in both groups, and a 2001 analysis by Christopher French and colleagues concluded there was no evidence of an effect above placebo.[2] Commentary in the Journal of Health Psychology notes that surveys of complementary medicine popularity are of limited value and that the key question is whether such practices do more good than harm.[5]

Some stones such as shungite contain heavy metals and can pose toxicity risks with prolonged handling or ingestion.[2] Reporting on Madagascar describes informal hand-dug rose quartz mines with very low pay.[2] In the UK, crystal healing is among the modalities represented by practitioner associations studied in work on the professionalisation of complementary medicine.[4]

timeline.event: John Dee reports receiving a crystal for scrying and healing, per Wikipedia.[2]
French and Williams run a quartz versus placebo-stone experiment.[2]
French and colleagues conclude no effect beyond placebo.[2]
Retail sales estimated above US$1 billion annually.[2]

lore.intro: Crystals appear in beauty and wellness communities as relaxation aids and skincare tools; discussion on general forums is often sceptical in tone.[2]

claims.claim: Stones balance energy and improve wellbeing
claims.believers: Practitioners say stones release blocked energy, lift mood and protect against negative energy, and report feeling calmer.[2]
claims.experts: Researchers report that volunteers given placebo stones reported the same effects as those with real quartz.[2]

claims.claim: Crystal facial rollers and tools improve skin
claims.believers: Users say stone rollers feel soothing and make the face look rested and less puffy.
claims.experts: No published studies have tested stone-specific effects on skin; relaxation and massage themselves are separate from mineral properties.

claims.claim: Shungite or other stones shield against radiation
claims.believers: Some promoters claim shungite absorbs electromagnetic radiation, including 5G.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the 5G claim as false and notes shungite can contain heavy metals.[2]
